questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Being registered at the university was okay - but it took time.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Online procedure, then a lot of waiting for them to produce a student card that didn't work.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The mobility office - but their suggestion was always to wait.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Not at all. I wasn't registered until December, when several of my classes had ended. This was due to the administration of the University of Bordeaux. First I followed classes at the economics faculty, but in October I was told that I wasn't supposed to follow classes there, contrary to what my counsellor told me. So I had to find new courses, get new pre-approvals, fill out a new OLA etc., etc.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be aware that you are only allowed to follow courses at the science faculty (if you are a science student at UCPH). Had I known this, I probably wouldn't have gone on exchange to Bordeaux.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Math courses were good. But I had expected to be allowed to follow econ. courses, so I was not satisfied with the academic programme.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The level of some of the math courses was what one could expect on a master's course. I had a 'Ethique et Management' course which was a joke.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Some of the teaching was quite similar, but I also experienced ancient, French-style copy-after-me kind of teaching which was just terrible.

questions.answer: Go to the pyrenees, biarritz, Le porge (the beach), maybe Ile de Ré. Cycling in the wine country outside bordeaux is awesome.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The French culture of denial

In France, denial is an art form, from the classroom to the parliament. It is not a denial of truth but of responsibility—a quiet refusal to acknowledge when something has gone wrong. Nowhere is this more evident than in the country’s proud tradition of public administration. Competition for entry into elite schools begins early. Years of hard work allow some of France’s brightest to study public administration - a degree that for many has led to ministry posts and, for a select few men, even the presidency. This obsession with public administration could lead one to think that the French might excel at it. Yet behind the polished façade lies a deeply rooted culture of denial—a habit of evading responsibility that seeps into everyday life.

I encountered this culture firsthand as an exchange student. After missing out on a spot at the acclaimed Université de Sorbonne, I enrolled at the Université de Bordeaux, a choice I hadn’t given much thought to, but one that probably meant speaking more French than in cosmopolitan Paris. My main goal was to revive the language I’d left behind a decade earlier, when I studied for a year in Nantes as a 15-year-old.

Participating in an exchange program through Erasmus can be a daunting task. Those who have tried it know the scale of bureaucracy that students need to conquer to participate in what can be an enlightening cultural exchange. But as I told the French Minister of Higher Education and Research, M. Philippe Baptiste, when I met him at the Erasmus headquarters in Bordeaux, the amount of exchange-related administrative work for the student “vaut le coût” - is worthwhile. In hindsight, I regret that well-intended white lie.

I have now “studied” for more than two months at the Université de Bordeaux. I am still not officially enrolled in any of my courses. Two or three times a week I show up in an empty classroom, not having been informed of changes to the timetable. This involves choosing a 30-ECTS course load that must be approved by one party at the University of Copenhagen, signed by another, and finally signed by the Université de Bordeaux. After following a series of interesting economics courses at the Faculty of Economics for five weeks, I was told by the French university’s administration that I would not receive credits for the courses. I had to leave the courses and find new ones, to my professors’ regret and to my own, in order to honor the 30-ECTS requirement. The Faculty of Science,
where I was registered, and the Faculty of Economics were apparently unable to transfer credits between each other, despite each faculty offering courses at the other.

This meant my Erasmus grant would not be transferred any time soon, since I had to fill out a completely new learning agreement - a process that would take weeks. Had I not been lucky enough to secure Danish grants, I would soon be joining the queues of less fortunate people receiving food handouts from local charities.

I spent my days emailing administrative personnel and showing up at the international mobility office, which was closed more often than not. A reply could be weeks in the making, if I was lucky enough to even get one. Most frequently, I was met by a version of “this is not our fault” spoken with the insouciance only the French muster. I was being kicked around and I was frankly appalled. As a 25-year-old master’s student from Denmark, this carelessness with respect to my time was a new and utterly stunning experience. To be fair, my French professors shared my frustrations and yet were not at all surprised by the ineffectiveness of the system.

Of course, bureaucracy frustrates outsiders everywhere, but in France the pattern seems particularly entrenched, not merely procedural but cultural. That instinct - to deflect responsibility – runs deep. In France, I think of it as a culture of denial: not denial of truth, but of responsibility. It extends from university offices to the highest levels of politics, shaping much of French administration.

The same impulse to deny responsibility appears in other domains. One striking example is the French refusal to acknowledge race - and therefore racial inequality. In my “Éthique et management” course, a discussion about bias in job interviews passed without a single mention of race. A hijab-wearing Black student, visibly dumbfounded, finally asked: “What about race?” The elderly white madame replied that in France, there is no such thing as race – everyone is simply French. Ah bon? I understand the historical roots of that reflex, but today it often serves to paper over the cracks of structural racial inequality. Again, a problem denied rather than confronted.

This culture of denial poses endless difficulties for international students like me, but its cost to French citizens is far greater. They are governed by people who refuse to compromise in order to move forward. France’s administrative paralysis isn’t merely procedural - it’s cultural. Until the
reflex of denial is replaced with a sense of shared responsibility, the country will remain caught between its administrative ideals and its bureaucratic reality. Bonne chance!
